title: How You Eat, Breathe & Sleep Sealed Inside Biosphere 2 for 2 Years
asof: Figures from 1991–1994 records · sources in description

shots.s: Eight people just walked into a glass box.
Then the door was sealed behind them.
The plan? Stay inside for two years.
No food from outside.
No water delivered.
Not even fresh air.
You're one of the eight.
Within months, you'll be hungry.
And the air itself starts to run out.
So how do you eat,
breathe,
and sleep,
inside a sealed world?
This is Biosphere 2.
It sits in the Arizona desert, north of Tucson.
It covers about three acres.
There are around sixty-five hundred windows.
Under the glass, there's a rainforest,
an ocean with a coral reef,
a marsh, a savanna, and a desert.
About thirty-eight hundred species went in with you.
It cost about a hundred and fifty million dollars.
Under the floor, a steel liner seals it from the ground.
Below that is a basement full of machines.
Pumps, fans and pipes keep it all alive.
If the power fails on a sunny day,
it can overheat within about twenty minutes.
On each side sits a giant lung.
When the air heats up, it expands.
The lung's roof rises, so the glass doesn't burst.
Then there's the farm.
And the little tower where you live.
The record for living sealed like this?
Six months, in Siberia.
You're going for two years.
Two weeks in, something goes wrong.
A crew member is running a rice machine.
It cuts off the tip of her finger.
The crew's doctor tries to fix it inside.
It's not enough.
So the door opens.
She leaves for surgery.
A few hours later, she walks back in.
And she carries a bag with her.
She later said it held a plant and a computer part.
Reporters only find out months later.
And it's not the only time the door opens.
Seeds, vitamins, even mousetraps come in.
So how sealed is it, really?
Rule number one: you eat what you grow.
The farm is about half an acre.
Eight people live off it.
You work it every single day.
There are goats for milk,
chickens and pigs,
and tilapia fish in tanks.
But mostly, you eat plants.
Sweet potatoes. A lot of sweet potatoes.
One crew member eats so many,
her skin turns orange.
Coffee grows in the rainforest.
There's enough for one cup every few weeks.
In the first six months, you average about seventeen hundred and eighty calories a day.
That's while doing hard farm work.
So you're hungry. All the time.
Plates get licked clean.
The men drop from about seventy-four kilos to sixty-two.
The women, from sixty-one to fifty-four.
The crew's doctor sees an upside.
He studies diets that cut calories.
Cholesterol drops by about a third.
Blood pressure drops too.
Over two years, the crew loses about seventeen percent of their weight.

d.small: body weight over 2 years · J Gerontol, 2002

shots.s: Most of it in the first eight months.
The glass was meant to hold a balanced world.
It doesn't stay balanced.
The hummingbirds die.
The honeybees die.
Most of the pollinating insects are gone.
Algae creeps over the coral reef.
But two things thrive.
Ants.
And cockroaches.
Soon they're everywhere.
Outside, air is about twenty-one percent oxygen.
Inside, that number starts falling.
Slowly. Month after month.
In 1992, a solar eclipse dims the sun.
The plants slow down, and the oxygen dips even faster.
By early 1993, it's down to about fourteen and a half.
That's like living high on a mountain.
Around fourteen or fifteen thousand feet up.
But you're in a desert, at under four thousand feet.
You're tired all the time.
Climbing stairs leaves you out of breath.
For months, some of you can't sleep properly.
Your breathing keeps stopping at night.
Safety rules call anything under nineteen and a half percent oxygen-deficient.
You're far below that.
So where is the oxygen going?
If something's using it up,
carbon dioxide should pile up.
It doesn't.
Scientists later find two culprits.
First, the rich farm soil.
Microbes in the soil eat oxygen,
and breathe out carbon dioxide.
Second, the concrete.
Bare concrete soaks up that carbon dioxide.
So the evidence vanishes into the walls.
In 1993, oxygen is pumped in from outside.
You can breathe easy again.
Critics say that breaks the whole idea of a sealed world.
Hungry. Tired. Low on air.
Eight people, one small tower.
And no way out.
The crew splits into two groups.
Some barely talk to each other.
But the work still gets done.
You keep farming.
You keep measuring.
One crew member later said the split never stopped the research.
You can email the outside world.
But nobody can come in to help.
September twenty-sixth, 1993.
Two years and twenty minutes after it closed,
the door opens.
You walk out thinner,
but alive, and all eight of you made it.
Was it a failure?
It showed how hard it is to build a world that works.
A second crew goes in, in 1994.
It ends after about six months, amid lawsuits.
Since 2011, the University of Arizona has owned Biosphere 2.
As of 2026, it's still used for research.
So, could you have lasted two years in there?
